data.text:
🔴 Why Japanese Soldiers Still Use Earplugs Instead of Modern Combat Ear Protection
— And Why That Needs to Change.
By Rie Ogasawara (Defense Journalist, President of the Association for Protecting SDF Personnel)
In Japan’s Self-Defense Forces (SDF), earplugs are still standard issue—not electronic earmuffs.
This is a serious problem.
Worldwide, modern militaries equip their troops with electronic earmuffs that can:
✔️ Block damaging explosions
✔️ Amplify voice commands and footsteps
✔️ Prevent blast pressure from injuring the brain
✔️ Keep commands secure from enemy surveillance

But in Japan, outdated practices persist.
Even during live-fire drills, soldiers are often forced to remove their earplugs to hear commands—risking permanent hearing loss.
In some units, earplugs aren’t even available. Soldiers have been given cotton wads instead.
And if they become hearing-impaired?
They’re told it’s their fault.
“You didn’t train hard enough.”
“Don’t complain. Others manage just fine.”

This isn’t just a health issue—it’s a strategic vulnerability.
Imagine a battlefield where soldiers can’t hear your orders… or where shouting out commands gives away your position.
In the 21st century, this level of unpreparedness is unacceptable.
Other countries—including the U.S., Philippines, and India—use electronic earmuffs as standard.
Only regimes like North Korea remain behind.
Even they, after recent deployments to assist Russian forces, may return with upgraded tactics and gear.
Japan is falling behind—not because it can’t afford it, but because of a misguided culture that rewards cost-cutting over human protection.
In SDF proposal contests, ideas that “require no budget” are praised more than those that protect lives.
This is not a story just for Japan.
It raises global questions:
▶ What kind of military do U.S. allies maintain?
▶ Can they operate safely in joint missions?
▶ Are soldiers seen as assets—or as disposable?
📌 Read the full article (in Japanese, but translatable via browser):
 Why Japan’s SDF Needs Modern Earmuffs—for Safety and Strategy
👉 https://t.co/4yKtmmeQJh
(¥330/month = about $2.10 USD; updated weekly)

Even if you don’t read Japanese, the issue is global—and the details shocking.

The public and the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Offices concerned are advised to MONITOR the weather condition and watch for the next warning to be issued at 2:00 AM tomorrow.

Alfred Rewane Road, particularly the stretch near the Registry and NNPC heading towards Golden Gate, is also experiencing some congestion, primarily attributed to alternation. 
Conversely, traffic movement remains good from Golden Gate, intersecting with Bayo Kuku Road and continuing inbound towards Osborne Foreshore. This favorable flow extends across Dolphin Bridge into Ilubirin and onto the Third Mainland Bridge at this time.

Finally, the Obalende Bridge and its immediate surroundings are currently reporting smooth traffic conditions.
No immediate road impediments have been observed, and our officers are present to manage the flow as needed.
